stops.name: Konya, the death of the Sultan of the Learned
stops.campa: Baha al-Din Walad dies in Konya in his seventies, having taught to the last, and the whole city is said to close its shops for his funeral: the sultan himself among the mourners, so great a crowd that the bier can barely pass through the streets to the rose garden set aside for the sultan's own family, where he is laid to rest. Jalal al-Din, twenty-three, inherits his father's students, his father's pulpit, and — though he does not fully know it yet — his father's unfinished path into the hidden sciences of the heart, which the young man has so far touched only through law and grammar.

stops.name: Konya, Rumi mounts the pulpit
stops.campa: The students of the dead master turn to the son, and Jalal al-Din takes up his father's chair: a young jurist and preacher already learned enough, by every outward measure, to be counted among the great teachers of the age, expounding Hanafi law and Qur'anic commentary to hundreds. He is respected, sought after, correct in every visible particular of the scholar's life. What his father's manuscripts, and his father's God, asked of a man beyond correctness he has not yet been shown; that showing is still thirteen years and one strange old wanderer away.

stops.name: Konya, Sayyid Burhan al-Din tests the son against the father
stops.campa: A dust-worn dervish arrives at Konya's gate: Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq of Termez, a former student of Baha al-Din's own youth, come from the east too late to see his teacher living. He goes first to weep at the grave, then seeks out the son, and delivers a verdict that unmans the young professor's confidence: in outward learning you have surpassed your father, but in the inward path, the science of states and stations that made him what he was, you are still lacking. Jalal al-Din, stung and humbled, submits himself as a disciple to his father's former student. Nine years of hidden schooling begin.
stops.quote: In learning you have surpassed your father, but in the inward path you are still lacking.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq (Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin; Mevlevi oral tradition)

stops.name: Aleppo and Damascus, the years of the Halawiyya and the circle of the shaykhs
stops.campa: On Burhan al-Din's order the young scholar goes south again, this time as a man, to complete his formal learning: years at the Halawiyya madrasa of Aleppo, seat of Hanafi jurisprudence, and after it in Damascus, where the greatest Sufis of the age are gathered. Tradition holds that he now sits among the discourses he only glimpsed as a child: the aging Shaykh al-Akbar Ibn al-Arabi, his brilliant stepson-disciple Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, who will one day be his neighbor and friend in Konya, and the controversial contemplative Awhad al-Din Kirmani. He returns west a finished jurist who has breathed the same rooms as the theorists of the Oneness of Being.

stops.name: Konya, the return, the forty-day seclusions, and the death of Burhan al-Din
stops.campa: Back in Konya, Burhan al-Din sets his pupil to a discipline no madrasa taught: chilla after chilla, forty-day seclusions of fasting and prayer in a locked cell, until the sayyid pronounces him complete, without equal in the world, he says, in the outward sciences as in the hidden ones, and releases him to teach on his own authority. Not long after, the old master dies at Kayseri. Jalal al-Din is now, in the eyes of Konya, everything a Sultan of the Learned's son should be: mufti to hundreds of students, jurist consulted by the city's judges, a man entirely respectable. He has no idea what is coming to unmake him.
stops.quote: Without equal in the world, in the outward sciences as in the hidden ones.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sayyid Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq on completing Rumi's training (Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin)

stops.name: Konya, the Inn of the Sugar Merchants, a stranger seizes the bridle
stops.campa: A wandering dervish in black felt, called Shams al-Din of Tabriz, the Flier, for he has never stayed anywhere long, comes to lodge at the Inn of the Sugar Merchants in Konya. As the renowned professor rides through the square surrounded by students, the stranger steps out and seizes his bridle: which is greater, he demands, the Prophet Muhammad, who said, we have not known You, God, as You should be known, or Bayazid Bistami, who said, glory be to me, how great is my station? Rumi, furious at the impertinence, answers that Muhammad's unknowing surpasses all Bayazid's claiming, and falls from his mount in a faint at the force of his own answer.
stops.quote: The Prophet's 'we have not known You as You should be known' surpasses Bayazid's 'glory be to me' — for Bayazid's thirst was small enough to be satisfied by a single drop, and he cried that he was full, while the Prophet's vessel could never be filled, and he thirsted on.
stops.quote_source: The traditional form of Rumi's answer to Shams of Tabriz, transmitted in Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin, and Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama

stops.name: Konya, the forty days behind the locked door
stops.campa: Rumi takes the stranger home. For forty days, by the account the order keeps, the two men shut themselves into a cell and see no one; food is passed through the door, and no word of what passes between them is ever fully told, only that a Sultan of the Learned's son emerges a different man, one to whom the outward sciences that made his name are now, he says, like carrion beside the feast Shams has set before him. Konya's foremost professor stops lecturing on law. His students, who had queued for his rulings, now find him instead composing verses and turning, unannounced, in the middle of the room.

stops.name: Konya, the disciples murmur, Shams reads the danger
stops.campa: The professor's abandonment of the pulpit for a penniless wanderer scandalizes Konya's learned circle. Students who once vied for his classes now find their teacher lost to them, closeted for days with a man of no lineage and no known school, who speaks to their master as an equal and sometimes as a master himself. Whispers turn to threats; some of the household, even, the tradition says, resent the stranger's hold on Rumi's heart. Shams, who has fled more cities than he has settled in, reads the coming danger in the mutterings at the door and, one winter night, without warning, is simply gone.

stops.name: Damascus, the first flight of the sun
stops.campa: Shams surfaces in Damascus, the city Rumi himself once studied in, and there he stays while, in Konya, the teacher he left behind falls into a grief the canon records almost as illness: weeks of silence, verses composed and destroyed, students turned away. Letters go out searching every direction. Word finally comes of the wanderer's whereabouts, and it is not Rumi himself but his own son, Sultan Walad, not yet twenty, who sets out on the road to Damascus to beg the sun of Tabriz to return and warm Konya again.

stops.name: Konya, Sultan Walad rides to bring him home
stops.campa: Sultan Walad finds Shams in Damascus and delivers his father's letters, written in verse, pleading and abject with love. Shams relents and returns with the young man, who, the son's own chronicle records with plain pride, walks the last miles on foot beside Shams's mount out of reverence, though offered a horse himself. Rumi and Shams are reunited in a scene the whole city gathers to watch, weeping, neither man able to say afterward which of them fell at the other's feet first. For a season the two are inseparable again, and the teaching of the pulpit is not resumed.
stops.quote: They fell at each other's feet, and no one knew who was the lover and who the beloved.
stops.quote_source: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama, on the reunion of Rumi and Shams (April 1247)

stops.name: Konya, the marriage of Shams and Kimya Khatun
stops.campa: To settle Shams among them and quiet the household's unease, Rumi arranges his marriage to Kimya Khatun, a girl raised since childhood in his own house, daughter of his second wife Kira Khatun by an earlier marriage. It is meant as an anchor, a reason for the wandering dervish to keep an address in Konya at last. But the marriage does not calm the jealousy circling Shams; within the household some still resent him bitterly for what he has taken from their teacher, and the bride herself, not yet strong, begins to fail under the strain of a house at war with itself around her.

stops.name: Konya, the last night, the cry in the dark
stops.campa: On a night in early winter, the account preserved by the order says, Shams and Rumi are sitting together when someone comes to the door and calls Shams out. He rises, saying to Rumi, I am called to be killed, and goes into the dark and is never seen alive again. Seven men, some say including Rumi's own second son Ala al-Din, are afterward named by rumor in his death; a body is said to have been found long after in a well near the house, and quietly laid, some accounts say, beside Baha al-Din Walad's own grave. The sun of Tabriz has set, this time for good.
stops.quote: I am called to be killed.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Shams of Tabriz on the night of his disappearance (Mevlevi oral tradition, later Ottoman-era chroniclers)
